claim: Concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) are responsible for cellular entry of nucleosides, which serve as precursors to nucleic acids and act as signaling molecules.
source: Concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) are responsible for cellular entry of nucleosides, which serve as precursors to nucleic acids and act as signaling molecules.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of CNTs, drawing from established scientific knowledge about nucleoside transporters.

claim: CNTs play a crucial role in the uptake of nucleoside-derived drugs, including anticancer and antiviral agents.
source: CNTs also play a crucial role in the uptake of nucleoside-derived drugs, including anticancer and antiviral agents.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is referenced in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: vcCNT is a CNT from Vibrio cholerae.
source: The crystal structure of a CNT from Vibrio cholerae (vcCNT) presents the first opportunity to examine specific nucleoside recognition by CNTs from a structural perspective (Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a citation to previous work.

claim: vcCNT utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs.
source: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study hCNTs: it utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs and shares high sequence identity (36–39%) with hCNTs with particularly high sequence identity for the nucleoside-binding site (64% with hCNT1, 73% with hCNT2, 91% with hCNT3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the functional properties of vcCNT.

claim: vcCNT shares 36-39% sequence identity with hCNTs.
source: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study hCNTs: it utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs and shares high sequence identity (36–39%) with hCNTs with particularly high sequence identity for the nucleoside-binding site (64% with hCNT1, 73% with hCNT2, 91% with hCNT3).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sequence similarity based on sequence analysis.

claim: vcCNT shares 64% sequence identity with hCNT1 at the nucleoside-binding site.
source: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study hCNTs: it utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs and shares high sequence identity (36–39%) with hCNTs with particularly high sequence identity for the nucleoside-binding site (64% with hCNT1, 73% with hCNT2, 91% with hCNT3).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sequence similarity at the binding site.

claim: vcCNT shares 73% sequence identity with hCNT2 at the nucleoside-binding site.
source: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study hCNTs: it utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs and shares high sequence identity (36–39%) with hCNTs with particularly high sequence identity for the nucleoside-binding site (64% with hCNT1, 73% with hCNT2, 91% with hCNT3).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sequence similarity at the binding site.

claim: vcCNT shares 91% sequence identity with hCNT3 at the nucleoside-binding site.
source: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study hCNTs: it utilizes a Na+ gradient for nucleoside transport like hCNTs and shares high sequence identity (36–39%) with hCNTs with particularly high sequence identity for the nucleoside-binding site (64% with hCNT1, 73% with hCNT2, 91% with hCNT3).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about sequence similarity at the binding site.

claim: vcCNT forms a homotrimer with each protomer possessing its own nucleoside-binding site and permeation pathway.
source: vcCNT forms a homotrimer with each protomer possessing its own nucleoside-binding site and permeation pathway (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: The vcCNT protomer adopts a new fold and is divided into two domains: the scaffold domain and the transport domain.
source: The protomer adopts a new fold and is divided into two domains: the scaffold domain that is responsible for trimerization and maintaining the overall architecture of the transporter (light blue, Figure 1B), and the transport domain where nucleoside binding and transport occur (other colors, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The scaffold domain is responsible for trimerization and maintaining the overall architecture of the transporter.
source: The protomer adopts a new fold and is divided into two domains: the scaffold domain that is responsible for trimerization and maintaining the overall architecture of the transporter (light blue, Figure 1B), and the transport domain where nucleoside binding and transport occur (other colors, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and previous work.

claim: The transport domain is where nucleoside binding and transport occur.
source: The protomer adopts a new fold and is divided into two domains: the scaffold domain that is responsible for trimerization and maintaining the overall architecture of the transporter (light blue, Figure 1B), and the transport domain where nucleoside binding and transport occur (other colors, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and previous work.

claim: The nucleoside-binding site is formed at the center of the transport domain between the tips of two helical hairpins (HP1 and HP2) and two partially unwound transmembrane helices (TM4 and TM7).
source: The nucleoside-binding site, facing the trimer axis, is formed at the center of the transport domain between the tips of two helical hairpins (HP1 and HP2) and two partially unwound transmembrane helices (TM4 and TM7) (Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure with citation to previous work.

claim: The structure of vcCNT-7C8C bound to uridine was solved at 2.1 Å resolution.
source: We solved the structure of a uridine-bound double mutant of vcCNT (Leu 7 to Cys and Ile 8 to Cys, termed 7C8C) at 2.1 Å, which is higher resolution than the 2.4-Å wild-type structure.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the resolution of the crystal structure.

claim: The vcCNT-7C8C structure revealed an additional water molecule in the binding site that bridges the 4-carbonyl of the uracil base with Glu 156.
source: The high-resolution mutant structure revealed another water in the binding site that bridges the 4-carbonyl of the uracil base with Glu 156 but was otherwise identical to the wild-type structure (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The vcCNT-7C8C mutations do not affect transporter function significantly.
source: The mutations do not affect transporter function significantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The KD of uridine for vcCNT is 36 μM.
source: We calculated the KD for uridine to be 36 μM (Figure 1D), which is similar to the reported Km values of uridine for hCNTs (Km = 22–80 μM), further suggesting that vcCNT is a good model system to study hCNTs (Molina-Arcas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The KD of uridine for vcCNT is similar to the reported Km values of uridine for hCNTs (Km = 22–80 μM).
source: We calculated the KD for uridine to be 36 μM (Figure 1D), which is similar to the reported Km values of uridine for hCNTs (Km = 22–80 μM), further suggesting that vcCNT is a good model system to study hCNTs (Molina-Arcas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature values with citation.

claim: hCNT1 mainly transports pyrimidines.
source: Human CNTs have differing nucleoside-base preferences: hCNT1 mainly transports pyrimidines, hCNT2 prefers purines, and hCNT3 is broadly selective for both pyrimidines and purines (Gray et al., 2004b; Molina-Arcas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citations.

claim: hCNT2 prefers purines.
source: Human CNTs have differing nucleoside-base preferences: hCNT1 mainly transports pyrimidines, hCNT2 prefers purines, and hCNT3 is broadly selective for both pyrimidines and purines (Gray et al., 2004b; Molina-Arcas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citations.

claim: hCNT3 is broadly selective for both pyrimidines and purines.
source: Human CNTs have differing nucleoside-base preferences: hCNT1 mainly transports pyrimidines, hCNT2 prefers purines, and hCNT3 is broadly selective for both pyrimidines and purines (Gray et al., 2004b; Molina-Arcas et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citations.

claim: The uracil base interacts with residues on HP1 (Gln 154 directly and Thr 155 and Glu 156 through water molecules) and TM4 (Val 188 via van der Waals interactions).
source: The uracil base interacts with residues on HP1 (Gln 154 directly and Thr 155 and Glu 156 through water molecules) and TM4 (Val 188 via van der Waals interactions).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Zebularine exhibits a ~threefold loss of binding affinity (KD = 120 μM) relative to uridine.
source: Zebularine exhibits a ∼threefold loss of binding affinity (KD = 120 μM) relative to uridine.
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The crystal structure of vcCNT bound to zebularine shows that the side chain of Glu 156 adopts a different rotamer position because it is unable to form the water-mediated interaction with the C4-carbonyl of the uracil base.
source: The crystal structure shows that the side chain of Glu 156 adopts a different rotamer position probably because it is unable to form the water-mediated interaction with the C4-carbonyl of the uracil base, consistent with the loss of binding affinity.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A with inference about the mechanism.

claim: 3-methyluridine has a KD of 520 μM for vcCNT.
source: We measured the affinity of vcCNT for 3-methyluridine, which contains a methyl group at this position that blocks the water-mediated interaction, and we found that it significantly decreased the binding affinity (KD = 520 μM, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Adenosine has a KD of 470 μM for vcCNT.
source: The purine nucleoside adenosine and the antiviral guanosine analog ribavirin also possess similarly weaker binding affinity (KD = 470 and 1530 μM, respectively).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Ribavirin has a KD of 1530 μM for vcCNT.
source: The purine nucleoside adenosine and the antiviral guanosine analog ribavirin also possess similarly weaker binding affinity (KD = 470 and 1530 μM, respectively).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The structures of vcCNT-7C8C bound to adenosine and ribavirin reveal that the bulky purine base displaces the water observed in the uridine structure while maintaining similar modes of ribose binding.
source: The structures reveal that the bulky purine base displaces the water observed in the uridine structure while maintaining similar modes of ribose binding, corroborating the idea that the reduced affinities of adenosine and ribavirin are due to the loss of the water-mediated interactions and highlighting the importance of the water coordinated by Thr 155 and Glu 156 in nucleoside recognition by CNTs.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structures shown in Figures 2C and 2D with inference about the mechanism.

claim: The KD of 5-fluorouridine for vcCNT is 16 μM.
source: To test the energetic contribution of substituents at the C5 position of the pyrimidine ring, we measured the KD for the anticancer drug 5-fluorouridine to be 16 μM, which is ∼twofold lower than the KD for uridine.
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: 5-fluorouridine has approximately twofold lower KD than uridine for vcCNT.
source: To test the energetic contribution of substituents at the C5 position of the pyrimidine ring, we measured the KD for the anticancer drug 5-fluorouridine to be 16 μM, which is ∼twofold lower than the KD for uridine.
evidence: This is a comparison of measured values from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The crystal structure of vcCNT-7C8C bound to 5-fluorouridine shows that the modified uracil base still fits into the nucleoside-binding site without any structural rearrangements of the protein.
source: The structure shows that the modified uracil base still fits into the nucleoside-binding site without any structural rearrangements of the protein.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 5-chlorouridine has a KD of 14 μM for vcCNT.
source: When another highly electronegative but slightly larger halogen, chlorine (3.16, 1.75 Å), is substituted at the C5 position, a similar KD is observed (14 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: 5-iodouridine has a KD of 58 μM for vcCNT.
source: However, when the large, weakly electronegative substituent iodine (2.66, 1.98 Å) or a methyl group (2.55, 2.00 Å) is added, we observe an increase in KD (∼60 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: 5-methyluridine has a KD of 61 μM for vcCNT.
source: However, when the large, weakly electronegative substituent iodine (2.66, 1.98 Å) or a methyl group (2.55, 2.00 Å) is added, we observe an increase in KD (∼60 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Smaller, highly electronegative substituents at the C5 position of uridine increase binding affinity for vcCNT.
source: In short, we observed an increase in affinity with smaller, highly electronegative substituents but a decrease in affinity with larger, less electronegative substituents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the measured KD values for different C5-substituted uridines.

claim: Larger, less electronegative substituents at the C5 position of uridine decrease binding affinity for vcCNT.
source: In short, we observed an increase in affinity with smaller, highly electronegative substituents but a decrease in affinity with larger, less electronegative substituents.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the measured KD values for different C5-substituted uridines.

claim: Phe 366 forms an offset π–π interaction with the aromatic pyrimidine ring.
source: Phe 366 forms an offset π–π interaction with the aromatic pyrimidine ring and also forms CH–π interactions with the ribose (Figure 1C, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figures 1C and 3A,B.

claim: Phe 366 forms CH–π interactions with the ribose.
source: Phe 366 forms an offset π–π interaction with the aromatic pyrimidine ring and also forms CH–π interactions with the ribose (Figure 1C, Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figures 1C and 3A,B.

claim: The addition of a small, highly electronegative substituent at the C5 position could strengthen the interaction between the pyrimidine ring and Phe 366.
source: The addition of a small, highly electronegative substituent at the C5 position could strengthen the interaction between the pyrimidine ring and Phe 366, as is the case with many π–π interactions (Hunter and Sanders, 1990; Ringer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural observations and literature on π–π interactions.

claim: Phe 366 is universally conserved between members of the CNT family.
source: Notably, Phe 366 is universally conserved between members of the CNT family, and its functional importance has never been tested.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence analysis of CNT family members.

claim: Mutation of Phe 366 to alanine results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine.
source: We found that the requirement for Phe at this position is strict, as mutation of this residue to alanine or tyrosine or tryptophan results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine while not affecting the stability significantly (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experiments shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Mutation of Phe 366 to tyrosine results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine.
source: We found that the requirement for Phe at this position is strict, as mutation of this residue to alanine or tyrosine or tryptophan results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine while not affecting the stability significantly (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experiments shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Mutation of Phe 366 to tryptophan results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine.
source: We found that the requirement for Phe at this position is strict, as mutation of this residue to alanine or tyrosine or tryptophan results in significantly decreased binding affinity for uridine while not affecting the stability significantly (Figure 3C–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ITC experiments shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: Phe 366 plays a critical role in recognition of the nucleoside by CNTs.
source: Therefore, we suggest that Phe 366 plays a critical role in recognition of the nucleoside by CNTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutagenesis and binding studies.

claim: Amino acid residues that interact with the ribose in the vcCNT structure (Glu 332, Asn 368, and Ser 371) are invariant between hCNTs and vcCNT.
source: Amino acid residues that interact with the ribose in the vcCNT structure (Glu 332, Asn 368, and Ser 371) are invariant between hCNTs and vcCNT.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence alignment of hCNTs and vcCNT.

claim: 3'-deoxyuridine has a KD greater than 2800 μM for vcCNT.
source: Both 3′- and 5′-deoxyuridine yielded KD values greater than 2800 μM (Figure 4A), while the binding affinity for 2′-deoxyuridine is not as drastically affected (KD = 170 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: 5'-deoxyuridine has a KD greater than 2800 μM for vcCNT.
source: Both 3′- and 5′-deoxyuridine yielded KD values greater than 2800 μM (Figure 4A), while the binding affinity for 2′-deoxyuridine is not as drastically affected (KD = 170 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: 2'-deoxyuridine has a KD of 170 μM for vcCNT.
source: Both 3′- and 5′-deoxyuridine yielded KD values greater than 2800 μM (Figure 4A), while the binding affinity for 2′-deoxyuridine is not as drastically affected (KD = 170 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The KD of gemcitabine for vcCNT is 1370 μM.
source: The measured KD of gemcitabine for vcCNT (KD = 1370 μM) is ∼22-fold higher than that for cytidine (KD = 61 μM) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The KD of cytidine for vcCNT is 61 μM.
source: The measured KD of gemcitabine for vcCNT (KD = 1370 μM) is ∼22-fold higher than that for cytidine (KD = 61 μM) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The KD of gemcitabine for vcCNT is approximately 22-fold higher than that for cytidine.
source: The measured KD of gemcitabine for vcCNT (KD = 1370 μM) is ∼22-fold higher than that for cytidine (KD = 61 μM) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of measured values from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: In the gemcitabine-bound structure, both Phe 366 and TM7b (including Ser 371) move slightly away from the nucleoside with respect to the uridine-bound structure.
source: In order for vcCNT to accommodate for the bulkier fluorine atom on the other epimeric position of C2′, which creates steric interference and electrostatic repulsion with the π electrons of Phe 366, both Phe 366 and TM7b (including Ser 371) move slightly away from the nucleoside with respect to the uridine-bound structure (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the gemcitabine-bound and uridine-bound crystal structures.

claim: The ribose of gemcitabine is reoriented with respect to the other nucleoside-bound structures.
source: Furthermore, the ribose of the gemcitabine is reoriented with respect to the other nucleoside-bound structures (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from comparing the gemcitabine-bound structure to other nucleoside-bound structures.

claim: Fluorine is a poor substitute for a hydroxyl as a hydrogen-bond acceptor.
source: In addition to the steric and electrostatic disruption of the ribose-binding site, fluorine is a poor substitute for a hydroxyl as a hydrogen-bond acceptor and thus provides a less favorable interaction of the ribose with Ser 371 (Howard et al., 1996; Dunitz and Taylor, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citations.

claim: Cytarabine has a KD greater than 3000 μM for vcCNT.
source: Cytarabine displayed no measurable binding when titrated into vcCNT (KD > 3000 μM).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: hCNTs show no significant binding and transport of cytarabine.
source: Interestingly, consistent with our observation with vcCNT, hCNTs show no significant binding and transport of cytarabine (Clarke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citation.

claim: Pyrrolo-cytidine has a KD of 0.9 μM for vcCNT.
source: Of all of the nucleosides and nucleoside analogs studied, the fluorescence probe pyrrolo-cytidine had the strongest binding affinity for vcCNT (KD = 0.9 μM, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The crystal structure of vcCNT-7C8C bound to pyrrolo-cytidine shows that the methylpyrrole ring fits neatly into a pocket formed by TM4 and TM6.
source: We solved the crystal structure of vcCNT-7C8C bound to pyrrolo-cytidine and found that the methylpyrrole ring fits neatly into a pocket formed by TM4 and TM6 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The nucleo-pocket is formed mainly by G187 (TM4), V188 (TM4), and L259 (TM6).
source: The vcCNT-7C8C nucleo-pocket, formed mainly by G187 (TM4), V188 (TM4), and L259 (TM6), is delineated with a dotted line.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Pyrrolo-gemcitabine has a KD of 24 μM for vcCNT.
source: We measured its binding affinity for vcCNT using the fluorescence-anisotropy assay and found that the KD decreased by ∼60-fold to 24 μM, suggesting that nucleobase interactions and ribose interactions are additive.
evidence: This is a measured value from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: The KD of pyrrolo-gemcitabine for vcCNT is approximately 60-fold lower than that of gemcitabine.
source: We measured its binding affinity for vcCNT using the fluorescence-anisotropy assay and found that the KD decreased by ∼60-fold to 24 μM, suggesting that nucleobase interactions and ribose interactions are additive.
evidence: This is a comparison of measured values from fluorescence anisotropy experiments.

claim: Nucleobase interactions and ribose interactions are additive in vcCNT binding.
source: We measured its binding affinity for vcCNT using the fluorescence-anisotropy assay and found that the KD decreased by ∼60-fold to 24 μM, suggesting that nucleobase interactions and ribose interactions are additive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the measured KD values for gemcitabine and pyrrolo-gemcitabine.

claim: hCNT1, hCNT3, and hENT1 are the main NTs that transport gemcitabine.
source: It is known that hCNT1, hCNT3, and hENT1 are the main NTs that transport gemcitabine (Marechal et al., 2009; Bhutia et al., 2011; Damaraju et al., 2012; Paproski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citations.

claim: Addition of 200 μM gemcitabine to hCNT3-expressing oocytes induced Na+ currents.
source: Addition of 200 μM gemcitabine to hCNT3-expressing oocytes induced Na+ currents (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 200 μM pyrrolo-gemcitabine had almost no effect on Na+ currents in hCNT3-expressing oocytes.
source: However, the same amount of pyrrolo-gemcitabine had almost no effect.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: hCNT3 binds to but does not transport pyrrolo-gemcitabine.
source: To resolve this issue, a mixture of equal concentrations of both compounds was added and a reduction of Na+ current was observed, suggesting that hCNT3 binds to but does not transport pyrrolo-gemcitabine.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiology experiments showing competitive inhibition.

claim: 200 μM pyrrolo-gemcitabine elicited approximately sevenfold higher total charge uptake than gemcitabine for hCNT1.
source: In contrast, 200 μM pyrrolo-gemcitabine elicited ∼sevenfold higher total charge uptake than gemcitabine for hCNT1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: hCNT2 transported neither gemcitabine nor pyrrolo-gemcitabine.
source: hCNT2 transported neither compound (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement about experimental results.

claim: The nucleo-pocket of vcCNT differs by only one amino acid (Gly 187 to Ser 374) from hCNT3.
source: The nucleo-pocket of vcCNT differs by only one amino acid (Gly 187 to Ser 374) from hCNT3 and three amino acids (Gly 187 to Ser 352, Val 188 to Leu 353, and Leu 259 to Val 424) from hCNT1.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence alignment of vcCNT, hCNT1, and hCNT3.

claim: The nucleo-pocket of vcCNT differs by three amino acids (Gly 187 to Ser 352, Val 188 to Leu 353, and Leu 259 to Val 424) from hCNT1.
source: The nucleo-pocket of vcCNT differs by only one amino acid (Gly 187 to Ser 374) from hCNT3 and three amino acids (Gly 187 to Ser 352, Val 188 to Leu 353, and Leu 259 to Val 424) from hCNT1.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence alignment of vcCNT, hCNT1, and hCNT3.

claim: Mutation of Val 375 and Leu 446 of hCNT3 to mimic the nucleo-pocket of hCNT1 leads to an increase in transport of pyrrolo-gemcitabine.
source: Consistent with our prediction, mutation of Val 375 and Leu 446 of hCNT3 to mimic the nucleo-pocket of hCNT1 leads to an increase in transport of pyrrolo-gemcitabine (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Mutation of Leu 353 and Val 424 of hCNT1 to mimic the nucleo-pocket of hCNT3 leads to a decrease in transport of pyrrolo-gemcitabine.
source: Furthermore, mutation of Leu 353 and Val 424 of hCNT1 to mimic the nucleo-pocket of hCNT3 leads to a decrease in transport of pyrrolo-gemcitabine (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The nucleoside-binding site of vcCNT has twofold pseudo-symmetry.
source: Two helical hairpins (HP1 and HP2) and two unwound helices (TM4 and TM7), related by twofold pseudo-symmetry, create a bowl-shaped nucleoside-binding site at the center of the transport domain of vcCNT (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The interactions with the nucleobase are mainly formed with HP1 and TM4b.
source: The interactions with the nucleobase are mainly formed with HP1 and TM4b, and the interactions with the ribose are mainly formed with HP2 and TM7b (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The interactions with the ribose are mainly formed with HP2 and TM7b.
source: The interactions with the nucleobase are mainly formed with HP1 and TM4b, and the interactions with the ribose are mainly formed with HP2 and TM7b (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ribose interactions are energetically important for CNT binding.
source: With regard to binding energetics, our equilibrium-binding studies have shown that the ribose interactions are energetically important consistent with previous non-equilibrium studies with hCNTs (Clarke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the equilibrium-binding studies with citation to previous work.

claim: The interaction between the C3′ ribose hydroxyl group and Ser 371 on TM7b is important in vcCNT.
source: For example, we showed that the interaction between the C3′ ribose hydroxyl group and Ser 371 on TM7b is important in vcCNT (Figures 1C and 4A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural and binding studies.

claim: The hCNT1S546P variant is non-functional.
source: Consistent with our observation, the hCNT1S546P variant is non-functional (Ser 546 in hCNT1 is equivalent to Ser 371 in vcCNT) (Cano-Soldado et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature with citation.

claim: Ser 546 in hCNT1 is equivalent to Ser 371 in vcCNT.
source: Consistent with our observation, the hCNT1S546P variant is non-functional (Ser 546 in hCNT1 is equivalent to Ser 371 in vcCNT) (Cano-Soldado et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence alignment.

claim: The loss of binding energy from modification of part of the nucleoside can be compensated for by the gain of energy from modification of another part of the nucleoside.
source: Another important finding of our studies is that interactions with the nucleobase and ribose can be additive, and thus the loss of binding energy from modification of part of the nucleoside can be compensated for by the gain of energy from modification of another part of the nucleoside.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the binding studies with gemcitabine and pyrrolo-gemcitabine.

claim: Phe 366 is the only residue within the nucleoside-binding site that forms interactions with both portions of the nucleoside.
source: Notably, Phe 366 is the only residue within the nucleoside-binding site that forms interactions with both portions of the nucleoside.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure.

claim: The role of Phe 366 is to position the nucleoside for effective binding thus serving as a 'selectivity ring'.
source: Taken together, we propose that the role of Phe 366 is to position the nucleoside for effective binding thus serving as a 'selectivity ring'.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural and binding studies.

claim: The transport domain undergoes a rigid-body motion while the scaffold domain, including TM6, remains static during the transition from the outward-occluded to the inward-occluded conformational state.
source: We previously proposed that the transport domain undergoes a rigid-body motion while the scaffold domain, including TM6, remains static during the transition from the outward-occluded to the inward-occluded conformational state (Figure 6C; Johnson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work with citation.

claim: In the inward-occluded conformation, TM6 (including Leu 259) is located on top of the bowl, serving as part of the intracellular gate and partially occluding the nucleoside from dissociating into the cytoplasm.
source: In the inward-occluded conformation, TM6 (including Leu 259) is located on top of the bowl, serving as part of the intracellular gate and partially occluding the nucleoside from dissociating into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the crystal structure with inference about function.

claim: Most of the interactions between transporter and nucleoside that are present in the inward-occluded structure are maintained in the outward-facing conformation.
source: This rigid-body conformational change also suggests that most of the interactions between transporter and nucleoside that are present in the inward-occluded structure are maintained in the outward-facing conformation, as observed with other sodium-coupled transporters (Reyes et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis and comparison to other transporters with citations.

claim: Amino acid residues that were shown to be important from inward-conformation-based binding studies in detergent have also been shown to be important for the binding and transport of nucleosides by human CNTs in several cell-based mutational studies.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, amino acid residues that were shown to be important from our inward-conformation-based binding studies in detergent have also been shown to be important for the binding and transport of nucleosides by human CNTs in several cell-based mutational studies (Loewen et al., 1999; Zhang et al., 2003, 2005; Yao et al., 2007; Slugoski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to literature with citations.

claim: vcCNT is an excellent model system to study human CNTs.
source: Although our CNT is prokaryotic in origin, it is an excellent model system to study human CNTs and offers us the opportunity to conduct structural studies of nucleoside and nucleoside-drug selectivity by hCNTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sequence and functional similarities between vcCNT and hCNTs.

claim: Pyrrolo-gemcitabine is transported more efficiently by hCNT1 than gemcitabine.
source: Furthermore, our electrophysiological studies show that it is not only transported more efficiently by hCNT1, but it is also selectively transported by hCNT1.

claim: Pyrrolo-gemcitabine is selectively transported by hCNT1.
source: Furthermore, our electrophysiological studies show that it is not only transported more efficiently by hCNT1, but it is also selectively transported by hCNT1.

claim: Destabilization of the inward-facing-occluded step would facilitate the release of pyrrolo-gemcitabine.

claim: Expression levels of hCNT1 are closely related to the responsiveness of many different types of normal or cancer cells to chemotherapy treatment.
source: Although our study with pyrrolo-gemcitabine serves merely as proof of concept, it is conceivable that the nucleo-pocket structure can be utilized in the design of nucleoside-derived drugs or prodrugs that can be specifically targeted only to cell types that express hCNT1 since expression levels of hCNT1 are closely related to the responsiveness of many different types of normal or cancer cells to chemotherapy treatment (Lane et al., 2010; Naito et al., 2010; Rabascio et al., 2010; Bhutia et al., 2011; Choi, 2012).
